overview: Legal & General ('L&G') is a UK-headquartered financial services group listed on the London Stock Exchange (GBp quote, GBP reporting) that provides pension risk transfer (PRT), retirement, protection and asset management solutions. The Group now operates through three core, synergistic businesses -- Institutional Retirement (global bulk annuities/PRT), Asset Management (LGIM, one of Europe's largest asset managers with public and private markets capabilities), and Retail (UK-market-leading workplace pensions, individual annuities and protection) -- having exited its non-retained US protection and PRT business via a sale to Meiji Yasuda Life completed in February 2026. L&G's roots date to 1836 and it describes its purpose as 'investing for the long term,' deploying both policyholder and shareholder capital into UK infrastructure, housing and private markets alongside running its core insurance and asset-management operations.

business_model.summary: L&G earns most of its economic profit as a specialist life insurer and asset manager rather than a general insurer. Institutional Retirement (formerly LGRI) writes bulk annuity/PRT contracts with UK and international defined-benefit pension schemes, taking on longevity and investment risk in exchange for a premium, then earning a long-duration spread between matched assets and annuity liabilities (released into profit over time as Contractual Service Margin, or CSM); 'asset optimisation' -- reinvesting the sovereigns-backed day-one portfolio into higher-spread credit and direct investments -- is an increasingly important source of profit. Retail sells individual annuities, protection (life, critical illness, income protection) and administers UK workplace defined-contribution (DC) pensions, again generating a store of future profit (CSM/risk adjustment) plus fee income from DC administration. Asset Management (LGIM) earns recurring management fees on c.£1.2 trillion of AUM, split between lower-margin index/passive/LDI mandates (often linked to L&G's own annuity and DC flows -- 'controlled distribution') and higher-margin, faster-growing Private Markets, international and solutions businesses. Revenue is therefore a mix of long-duration insurance-liability profit emergence (highly recurring, multi-decade) and AUM-based asset-management fees (recurring but market-level sensitive), supplemented by new-business margin on PRT/annuity writing (transactional/cyclical, dependent on market volumes and pricing discipline). The non-retained US protection and PRT business (sold to Meiji Yasuda, completed February 2026) generated a £1,398m IFRS gain on disposal recognised in H1 2026 and freed Solvency II capital for an additional £1bn/£1.2bn buyback; Meiji Yasuda also took a 5% economic interest in L&G and the companies plan a continuing US PRT product partnership via Banner Life.

revenue_streams.name: Asset Management (LGIM fee and balance-sheet income)
Group/Corporate (debt costs, investment projects, Corporate Investments unit run-off)

business_model.customer_type: Mixed: B2B with corporate DB pension scheme trustees/sponsors and institutional clients (PRT, LGIM institutional mandates); B2B2C via employer-sponsored workplace pensions and group protection; B2C retail customers for individual annuities, protection and equity release/lifetime mortgages; c.12.1 million Retail customers and c.£236bn of UK DC assets under administration.
business_model.geographic_mix: Predominantly UK (PRT, Retail, UK DC, UK-domiciled LGIM AUM); international exposure through Global PRT (US PRT via the Meiji Yasuda partnership, and other international markets), and LGIM's growing international/Asia AUM (£547bn of 'International assets' within the £1.24tn total AUM at H1 2026). The divestiture of the non-retained US protection/PRT entity in February 2026 reduced direct US insurance-liability exposure, though a US PRT origination partnership with Meiji Yasuda continues via Banner Life.

competitive_position.market_position: Historically the largest or joint-largest writer of UK bulk annuities/PRT (c.20-27% share in recent years and the UK's largest open-market individual annuity provider and largest DC provider), but competitive intensity has increased sharply: in H1 2026, Rothesay overtook L&G for UK PRT market leadership (Rothesay c.28% share vs. L&G c.18%), reflecting both L&G's deliberate pricing discipline (14% minimum IRR hurdle) and more aggressive competitor pricing. LGIM remains one of Europe's largest asset managers (c.£1.2tn AUM) but faces intense fee pressure from scale passive managers (BlackRock, Vanguard, State Street) in its large index/LDI book, offset by a strategic pivot toward higher-margin Private Markets (£79bn AUM, targeting £85bn+ by 2028) and international distribution.

moat_factors.description: c.98% of UK PRT volumes are transacted with long-standing LGIM clients, c.90% of annuity assets and c.95% of Workplace AUA are managed in-house by LGIM, and over half of Asset Management's net new revenue is sourced from controlled distribution (PRT, annuities, Workplace flows) -- a structural advantage over asset managers or insurers lacking an integrated retirement/asset-management platform.

moat_factors.factor: Scale and underwriting/actuarial expertise in longevity risk
moat_factors.description: Decades of accumulated longevity, mortality and pricing data plus large in-force back books (£9.0bn Institutional Retirement store of future profit, £4.0bn Retail) create underwriting and asset-sourcing expertise that is difficult for new entrants to replicate quickly.

moat_factors.factor: Asset origination / direct investment capability ('asset optimisation')
moat_factors.description: A sovereigns-based day-one investment strategy followed by active rotation into higher-spread credit, direct investments and private assets is generating a growing, differentiated profit stream (guidance raised to >£400m p.a. from £300m), supported by LGIM's in-house credit and private markets capabilities.

moat_factors.factor: Brand and distribution reach in UK retail/workplace
moat_factors.description: UK's largest DC provider (>£200bn AUM) with a 99% scheme retention rate and new distribution partnerships (e.g., HSBC UK for annuities) support customer acquisition, though switching costs for DC scheme sponsors and individual annuity customers are only moderate.

Solvency II coverage ratio of 201% (H1 2026), comfortably above the 160-190% target range, provides flexibility to write new PRT business and fund capital returns, though this strength is itself a function of a still-evolving, favourable UK capital regime (Solvency UK matching-adjustment reforms) rather than a durable, competitor-proof advantage.

weaknesses: Lost PRT market leadership to Rothesay in H1 2026 as competitors price more aggressively, raising the risk that disciplined IRR hurdles (14% minimum) cost L&G market share and scale benefits over time

LGIM's large legacy index/LDI book faces structural fee compression from larger global passive managers (BlackRock, Vanguard, State Street), requiring continued mix-shift to Private Markets to sustain margin (average fee margin still only 9.6bps vs. a 2028 ambition of double digits)

Complexity from historic acquisitions and a decade of organic growth prompted a September 2026 restructuring targeting c.1,000 job cuts (c.10% of headcount) by mid-2027, indicating execution and change-management risk

Exited US protection/PRT business removes a geographic diversification source and concentrates the Group's insurance risk more heavily on the UK economic, regulatory and demographic cycle, even as a smaller US PRT origination partnership continues via Meiji Yasuda/Banner Life

growth_drivers: Structural UK DB-to-PRT pipeline: trustees of the large majority of UK DB schemes (many now in surplus) continue to seek buy-ins/buyouts, with a long-term UK PRT market expected to run at £45-50bn+ p.a.; L&G targets £50-65bn of cumulative UK PRT volumes 2024-2028 at sub-4% strain

Workplace DC structural growth: DC assets under administration up 27% YoY to £128bn (H1 2026) as the DB-to-DC shift continues; L&G targets doubling Workplace assets by 2034 and capturing a share of the c.£20bn individual annuity decumulation opportunity

Asset Management mix-shift to higher-margin Private Markets and international distribution: Private Markets AUM up to £79bn (H1 2026, targeting £85bn+ by 2028), record Annualised Net New Revenue (ANNR) of £23m in H1 2026, and a cost-income ratio improving to 71% en route to a sub-70% target and an Asset Management operating profit target of £500-600m by 2028

Asset optimisation / active balance-sheet management across the growing £90.9bn Annuity Portfolio, with IFRS profit guidance raised to >£400m p.a. (from £300m) and further upside from credit spread widening

Strategic partnerships to expand private credit and wealth-channel reach: the July 2025 Blackstone partnership (public-private credit solutions) and the Meiji Yasuda partnership (5% L&G economic stake holder, continuing US PRT origination via Banner Life, and asset-management collaboration)

Capital-light buy/build/partner M&A in Private Markets (Proprium Capital Partners 75% stake acquired 2025, adding European/Asia-Pacific real estate reach; Pemberton and NTR stakes) to deepen private credit, real estate and infrastructure capabilities

Capital return programme: >£5bn planned 2025-2027 shareholder returns (progressive 2% p.a. dividend growth plus a £1.2bn share buyback, partly funded by Meiji Yasuda sale proceeds and Corporate Investments unit disposals), supporting EPS and per-share metrics even if absolute profit growth is more modest
Simplification/cost programme targeting c.1,000 role reductions (c.10% of headcount) by mid-2027 to reduce organisational complexity and redeploy savings into growth areas

business.risk: Loss of UK PRT market leadership / pricing discipline trade-off
business.description: Rothesay overtook L&G as the largest UK PRT writer in H1 2026 (c.28% vs. c.18% share); L&G's strict 14% minimum IRR hurdle rate is deliberate but risks ceding scale, back-book growth and asset-management flow-through to more aggressive competitors if pricing stays competitive for an extended period.

Average Asset Management revenue margin of only 9.6bps (H1 2026) reflects a large low-margin passive/LDI/index book exposed to fee competition from BlackRock, Vanguard and State Street; the 2028 ambition of reaching double-digit bps margins depends on continued successful mix-shift to Private Markets and international/wholesale channels.

business.risk: Execution risk on the c.1,000-role restructuring
business.description: The September 2026 announcement to cut roughly 10% of headcount by mid-2027 (excluding Asset Management, which has its own restructuring) carries delivery, morale, union-negotiation and one-off cost risk, alongside the broader simplification agenda following the Meiji Yasuda carve-out.

Large individual PRT transactions can be lumpy and schemes may delay or split large deals (management flagged UK 2026 market volumes likely below the previously anticipated £50bn, with some large transactions slipping into 2027), creating revenue/new-business timing volatility.

financial.risk: Solvency II / Solvency UK capital ratio normalisation
financial.description: The Solvency II coverage ratio (201% at H1 2026) is well above the 160-190% target operating range and is expected to converge toward that range as capital is deployed into new PRT business and buybacks, which reduces the capital buffer against adverse longevity, credit or market shocks over time.

H1 2026 results included £(344)m of adverse economic impacts on the insurance portfolio from short/medium-term inflation expectation volatility, property mark-to-market movements and other market items, illustrating that IFRS profit before tax remains sensitive to period-to-period market and assumption changes even though core operating profit is more stable.

financial.risk: Solvency II debt leverage and interest cost
financial.description: SII debt leverage stood at 33.9% at 30 June 2026 (seasonally elevated due to dividend timing and upfront recognition of the full £1.2bn buyback), with management expecting a medium-term downward trajectory as Own Funds grow; Group debt costs of £114m in H1 2026 are a structural drag on core operating profit.

SII operational surplus generation (OSG) per share is expected to grow at >5% CAGR (2025-27) against 2% p.a. dividend growth, with management targeting SII net surplus generation covering the dividend by 2027 under normal new-business-strain scenarios -- implying cover is not yet fully established today.

regulatory.risk: Solvency UK / matching adjustment regime changes
regulatory.description: The PRA's ongoing reform of the UK matching adjustment and wider Solvency UK regime (post-Brexit divergence from EU Solvency II) changes the eligible asset and liability universe for annuity writers; while recent reforms have generally been accommodative for PRT writers, any tightening of MA rules, capital charges or asset eligibility would directly affect L&G's largest risk exposure (Institutional Retirement).

regulatory.risk: UK life insurance capital requirement changes
regulatory.description: The Group explicitly flags that changes in capital requirements, including evolving Insurance Capital Standards, could impact its reported solvency position and its dividend/capital return policy -- a direct link between regulatory change and shareholder returns.

regulatory.risk: Conduct, consumer protection and 'Targeted Support'/advice regulation
regulatory.description: FCA initiatives such as Targeted Support and the Pure Protection Market Study, alongside Senior Managers and Certification Regime reform, create ongoing compliance cost and potential conduct-risk exposure across Retail protection, annuities and workplace pensions.

regulatory.risk: Cross-border regulatory complexity from the Meiji Yasuda partnership
regulatory.description: The continuing US PRT origination partnership (via Banner Life) and Meiji Yasuda's 5% economic stake in L&G introduce a smaller, but new, layer of cross-border regulatory and governance coordination despite the direct divestiture of the US insurance entity.

macro.risk: Interest rate and credit spread sensitivity of the annuity book
macro.description: L&G's largest business (Institutional Retirement) is built on long-duration matched assets and liabilities; falling long-term UK gilt/credit yields increase annuity liability values and can compress new-business margins, while credit spread widening (a tail risk in a downturn) creates both credit-loss risk on the matching portfolio and upside 'asset optimisation' opportunity -- management explicitly notes asset-optimisation profit has further upside from material credit spread widening, underscoring the two-sided macro sensitivity.

macro.risk: UK economic growth, inflation and demographic/longevity trends
macro.description: Longevity improvements or deteriorations directly affect reserving for PRT, individual annuities and protection liabilities; L&G called out high volatility in short-to-medium-term UK inflation expectations as a driver of H1 2026 investment variance.

macro.risk: Equity and credit market levels affecting AUM-linked fee income
macro.description: LGIM's management fee revenue is a function of average AUM, which is itself sensitive to global equity and bond market performance; a sustained market downturn would reduce fee revenue and could trigger net outflows from more price-sensitive institutional mandates (as already seen with £(25.1)bn of net outflows in H1 2026, concentrated in lower-margin Asia institutional mandates).

macro.risk: Climate-related transition and physical risk to investment portfolio
macro.description: As a large asset owner (c.£108bn of proprietary assets) and asset manager (c.£1.2tn AUM), L&G is exposed to transition risk (stranded/downgraded assets in carbon-intensive sectors) and physical risk (extreme weather affecting real estate and infrastructure investments), managed via scenario analysis and decarbonisation targets but not eliminated.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: The UK pension risk transfer market remains structurally large and growing (consultants estimate full-year 2026 volumes of £35-45bn+, sustaining at £45-50bn p.a. over the medium term) as the vast majority of UK DB schemes are now in surplus and seeking to de-risk via buy-in/buyout; competition has intensified meaningfully in 2026 (Rothesay overtaking L&G in H1 2026 share), which should keep pricing competitive but also signals continued strong structural demand. UK workplace DC assets continue to compound as auto-enrolment matures and the Mansion House Accord pushes more DC capital toward private/growth assets, a structural tailwind for both Retail workplace administration and LGIM private markets. Global asset management faces ongoing fee compression in passive/index strategies but continued growth in private markets, ETFs and international distribution.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate. Institutional Retirement and Retail protection/annuity new-business volumes are influenced by the economic cycle (corporate pension funding levels, gilt yields, consumer demand for annuities/protection) but the large in-force back book (CSM/RA store of future profit of £13.0bn) provides a highly recurring, multi-decade profit-emergence stream that smooths cyclicality versus a pure new-business writer. Asset Management fee income is directly linked to AUM and market levels, making it the most market/cycle-sensitive segment.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High for the annuity/PRT book: falling long-term rates raise the present value of long-duration liabilities and can pressure new-business margins, though matched asset-liability management (sovereigns-based strategies, direct investment/asset optimisation) mitigates much of the balance-sheet risk; a higher-for-longer rate environment has generally supported the attractiveness of annuities to retail/DB customers and supported new-business margins in 2025-2026.
key_input_costs: Credit spreads and default experience on matching-adjustment assets
Regulatory capital costs under Solvency UK

recent_developments.event: Announced plans to cut approximately 1,000 roles (c.10% of workforce, excluding Asset Management) by mid-2027 via an initial voluntary-redundancy process, as CEO António Simões cited a decade of accumulated organisational complexity rather than financial distress as the driver.

Commenced the second tranche of the £1.2bn share buyback programme (to run to c.March 2027) after completing the first £600m tranche (12 March-11 September 2026, c.225.5m shares repurchased at an average 266.07p).

H1 2026 results: Core Operating Profit up 7% to £918m, Core Operating EPS up 11% to 12.15p (above the 6-9% target range); IFRS profit before tax of £1,997m driven by a £1,398m gain on the Meiji Yasuda disposal; raised full-year 2026 asset-optimisation profit guidance to >£400m p.a. (from £300m) and raised FY2026 core operating EPS growth expectations to above the top end of the 6-9% target range; Solvency II coverage ratio of 201%, OSG of £790m (+3%); confirmed 2% interim dividend increase to 6.24p.

Completed the sale of the non-retained US protection and PRT business to Meiji Yasuda Life for $2.3bn equity value (announced February 2025), generating c.£1.2bn of Solvency II capital and an IFRS gain above £1.3bn; Meiji Yasuda took a 5% economic interest in L&G and the two companies formed a continuing US PRT origination partnership via Banner Life; proceeds funded an incremental £1bn of shareholder returns, lifting the 2026 buyback to £1.2bn in total.

Scott Wheway (former Scottish Widows Group chair) joined the L&G board as chair-designate on 2 January 2026 and succeeded Sir John Kingman as Group Chair following the AGM on 21 May 2026, after Kingman's nine-year tenure.

Competitive UK PRT market: Rothesay overtook L&G for UK PRT market leadership in H1 2026 (Rothesay c.28% share vs. L&G c.18%), with analysts (e.g., RBC) flagging the more competitive PRT pricing environment as a risk to L&G's medium-term earnings forecasts; L&G maintained its 14% minimum IRR hurdle rather than chase volume.

Announced a strategic partnership with Blackstone to develop public-private credit solutions, combining Blackstone's private credit platform with LGIM's active fixed income capabilities, aimed at expanding wealth/wholesale distribution and supporting the US annuity-matching asset pipeline.

Continued disposal of the Corporate Investments unit (18 non-strategic assets sold since June 2024, c.£500m of assets remaining at H1 2026), with proceeds redeployed to the buyback programme and core-business growth; management expects to have materially exited the unit by end-2027.

guidance.management_commentary: CEO António Simões described H1 2026 as evidence of 'becoming a simpler, more focused L&G,' highlighting 7% core operating profit growth, 11% core operating EPS growth, c.£450m of the £1.2bn buyback completed, improved dividend cover and a 2% interim dividend increase. Management emphasised the standout performance of Asset Management (37% fee-related earnings growth, record ANNR, reduced cost-income ratio) and reaffirmed strict pricing discipline (14% minimum IRR hurdle) in a more competitive Institutional Retirement market even as overall UK PRT market volumes in 2026 are now expected to fall short of the previously flagged £50bn. The subsequent September 2026 announcement of c.1,000 job cuts (10% of headcount) by mid-2027 reflects management's explicit view that a decade of growth left the organisation too complex, requiring further simplification even against a backdrop of strong headline earnings growth.

bull_case: Synergistic 'flywheel' model (c.98% of UK PRT with existing LGIM clients, c.90-95% of annuity/Workplace assets managed in-house) gives L&G structural cost and distribution advantages that pure-play competitors in PRT or asset management individually lack

Multiple medium-term growth engines are tracking at or above target: core operating EPS growth above the top of the 6-9% range, Asset Management fee-related earnings up 37% YoY, record ANNR, and asset-optimisation guidance raised twice (to >£400m p.a.) reflecting genuine earnings upside beyond the base PRT/CSM-release business

Attractive, de-risked capital return story: >£5bn planned 2025-2027 shareholder returns (progressive dividend plus £1.2bn buyback), funded in part by the Meiji Yasuda US divestiture proceeds and ongoing Corporate Investments unit disposals, with a Solvency II coverage ratio (201%) comfortably above the 160-190% target range providing a large capital buffer

Simplification following the US exit (three core businesses, c.1,000 planned role reductions) should structurally lower the cost base and sharpen management focus on higher-return UK/global PRT, Retail and Private Markets growth

Structural UK tailwinds remain intact: the large majority of UK DB schemes are in surplus and still transitioning to PRT, DC assets keep compounding via auto-enrolment, and growing allocations to private markets (Mansion House Accord, PMAF) support both Retail and LGIM over the next decade
bear_case: L&G has lost UK PRT market leadership to Rothesay in H1 2026 (c.18% vs. c.28% share), and maintaining strict 14% IRR pricing discipline in a more competitive market risks a slower-growing back book, lower asset-management flow-through and analyst earnings downgrades (e.g., RBC cutting forecasts across all three divisions)

LGIM's large passive/index/LDI book carries structural fee pressure from larger-scale global managers (BlackRock, Vanguard, State Street); the current 9.6bps average fee margin is well below the 2028 double-digit-bps ambition, making the growth plan dependent on continued successful (and competitive) mix-shift into Private Markets

The September 2026 announcement of c.1,000 job cuts (10% of headcount) signals underlying organisational complexity and execution risk even as headline results look strong, and restructuring costs/management distraction could weigh on near-term delivery

IFRS profit before tax remains volatile around the more stable core operating profit measure (e.g., £(344)m of adverse economic/insurance-portfolio impacts in H1 2026), and the business's long-duration annuity liabilities remain sensitive to interest rate, credit spread and longevity assumption changes that are largely outside management's control

Divesting the non-retained US protection/PRT business concentrates L&G's insurance risk more heavily on the UK regulatory (Solvency UK/PRA matching-adjustment reform), demographic and economic cycle, removing a geographic diversification source even as a smaller US PRT origination partnership continues via Meiji Yasuda/Banner Life
